about: Plain-word tooltips for the app (FIF-D15-DAT). Each term has a short tooltip and the data columns it explains. Rules and how to add a term: data_notes.md section 11.

terms.tooltip: The lowest oxygen level, in %, at which something can keep burning. A lower LOI means it burns more easily, so it is riskier. Earth's air is about 21% oxygen. FLEX measured LOI for fuel droplets at different pressures.
How fast a flame moves along a material, in millimetres per second (mm/s). Faster spread means a fire grows faster, so it is riskier. Only the 2 Saffire-II SIBAL samples have a measured spread rate.
The flame spread rate divided by the airflow speed (both in mm/s), so it has no unit. It lets you compare spread in different airflows. Filled only for the 2 SIBAL samples.
How much of the gas around the flame is oxygen. Earth's air is about 21%. Min and max are the lowest and highest levels tested; they are the same when only one level was used.
How hard the surrounding gas presses, in kilopascals. Earth's air at sea level is about 101 kPa (1 atmosphere). Empty for Saffire-II and BASS-II, whose tables give no pressure.

How fast air moves past the flame, in cm/s. In space hot air doesn't rise, so moving air brings the flame fresh oxygen. FLEX burned in still air (0). BASS-II's lowest speed is empty when it was turned down further than noted.
The near-weightless state on the space station. Hot air doesn't rise, so flames get oxygen only by slow mixing or from moving air, and they burn differently than on Earth.

FLEX and FLEX-2 burned small fuel droplets on the space station. Saffire-II burned large samples in an empty cargo ship. BASS-II burned small solid samples in a wind tunnel on the station, changing airflow and oxygen.
What was burned: a liquid fuel droplet (FLEX, FLEX-2) or a solid sample (Saffire-II, BASS-II).
The kind of material: hydrocarbon or alcohol (liquid fuels), or plastic, fabric, silicone or wax (solids). Unknown: BASS-II samples whose material is never named.
How a test ended. Extinction: the flame went out. Completion: the fuel burned away. Disruption: cut short. Blowoff: blown out by strong air. No ignition: never lit. Empty: not recorded.
Out of the FLEX tests that finished, the share where the fuel burned away instead of the flame going out. 1 means every flame kept burning. Cut-short tests are left out.

A gas added to make a fire harder to keep going. FLEX tested CO2, helium and SF6. The table shows which gas was added (none = no suppressant) and its share of the gas in %. Empty for FLEX-2, whose table doesn't say.
How many tests in this group had CO2 or helium added. Flames go out more often with a suppressant, so a group with many of these keeps burning less.
A faint, low-temperature flame that is hard to see. In FLEX, some fuel droplets kept burning this way after the visible flame went out.
Concurrent: the air flows the same way the flame spreads. Opposed: the air flows against it. Saffire-II used both.
A clear acrylic plastic, often sold as Plexiglas.
A fabric woven from cotton and fiberglass.
A fire-resistant fabric, the kind used in firefighters' suits.
